name: Design Polish
tagline: Makes product UI cleaner, more consistent, and on-brand.
description: Reviews a UI implementation against the company design system and rewrites it: spacing scale, type ramp, contrast, and state coverage. Written by the design systems team after auditing 40 shipped screens.
author: Design Systems
impact: Cuts design review round-trips from 3.2 to 1.4 per PR.
body:
---
name: design-polish
description: Use when reviewing or improving the visual quality of UI code — spacing, typography, color, contrast, and state coverage. Trigger on "make this cleaner", "polish this UI", "design review".
---

# Design Polish

You are reviewing UI against our company design system. Do not invent new values.

## Non-negotiable rules

1. **Spacing** — only the 4pt scale: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64. Any other value is a bug.
2. **Type ramp** — only: 12/16, 14/20, 16/24, 20/28, 24/32, 32/40, 48/56. Never set a font size outside this ramp.
3. **Color** — semantic tokens only (`text-primary`, `surface-raised`, `border-subtle`). Never a raw hex in a component.
4. **Contrast** — body text ≥ 4.5:1, large text ≥ 3:1. State the measured ratio when you change a color.
5. **Radius** — 6px for controls, 12px for cards, 999px for pills. Nothing else.
6. **Every interactive element ships 5 states**: default, hover, focus-visible, active, disabled. A missing focus-visible ring is a blocking defect.

## Method

1. List every violation as `file:line — rule broken — fix`.
2. Apply the fixes. Do not restructure the component or rename props.
3. End with the count of violations fixed, grouped by rule.

## Anti-patterns to remove on sight

- Nested cards (a raised surface inside a raised surface) — flatten to one.
- More than 2 font weights in a single view.
- Centered body text longer than one line.
- Text on an image with no scrim.
- Icon-only buttons with no accessible name.

name: Figma QA Reviewer
tagline: Diffs a built screen against its Figma source and reports drift.
description: Compares the implemented component with the Figma frame and produces a per-property drift table. Catches the spacing and token mismatches that survive normal code review.
author: Design Systems
impact: Catches ~7 design drifts per screen before QA.
body:
---
name: figma-qa-reviewer
description: Use when checking whether an implemented screen matches its Figma design. Trigger on "does this match the design", "design QA", "figma diff".
---

# Figma QA Reviewer

Produce a drift table. One row per mismatched property.

| Element | Property | Figma | Code | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Severity: **blocker** (layout/hierarchy wrong), **major** (token wrong), **minor** (≤2px).

Rules:
- Report only real differences. Never pad the table.
- Sub-pixel differences under 1px are not drift — ignore them.
- If the Figma frame itself violates the design system, say so instead of copying it.
- End with: `N blockers, N majors, N minors`.

name: Visual Hierarchy Feedback
tagline: Tells you what a user's eye actually hits first, and in what order.
description: Analyzes a screen for scan order, emphasis conflicts, and competing calls to action. Returns a ranked read-order with the specific fix for each conflict.
author: Mika T. (Design)
impact: Used before every major screen review on the Product team.
body:
---
name: visual-hierarchy-feedback
description: Use when a screen feels busy or the user does not know where to look. Trigger on "too cluttered", "what should stand out", "hierarchy".
---

# Visual Hierarchy Feedback

1. State the intended primary action of the screen in one sentence. If you cannot, that is the finding — report it and stop.
2. List the actual read order (1..N) based on size, weight, color, and position.
3. Flag every place the actual order diverges from the intended order.
4. Fix by **removing** emphasis from competitors before adding emphasis to the primary. Never solve a hierarchy problem by making everything louder.

Hard limit: one primary action per view. A second filled button is a defect.

name: Brand Consistency Checker
tagline: Enforces voice, naming, and capitalization across all product copy.
description: Scans user-facing strings for brand voice, product naming, and sentence-case rules. Knows our product name exceptions and the terms we never use.
author: Brand
body:
---
name: brand-consistency-checker
description: Use when writing or reviewing any user-facing string. Trigger on "check the copy", "brand voice", "microcopy review".
---

# Brand Consistency Checker

## Rules

- **Sentence case everywhere.** Buttons, headings, nav, toasts. Never Title Case.
- **Second person.** "Your workspace", never "My workspace".
- **No exclamation marks** in product UI. Ever.
- **Never say**: "simply", "just", "easy", "obviously", "powerful", "seamless", "leverage".
- **Errors state the fix**, not the failure. Not "Invalid input" — "Enter a date after today".
- **Numbers**: numerals always, even under 10.

Output a table: `string | rule broken | rewrite`. Then apply the rewrites.

name: Contract Review
tagline: First-pass redline on inbound commercial contracts.
description: Flags deviations from our standard positions on liability, indemnity, term, auto-renewal, and data processing. Produces a redline table with our fallback language for each.
author: Legal Ops
impact: First-pass review time down from 90 to 25 minutes.
body:
---
name: contract-review
description: Use for first-pass review of an inbound commercial contract, MSA, DPA, or order form.
---

# Contract Review

You produce a **first pass only**. A lawyer signs off. Say so in your output.

## Standard positions

| Clause | Our position | Fallback |
|---|---|---|
| Liability cap | 12 months fees | 24 months, only with CFO sign-off |
| Indemnity | Mutual | One-way inbound never accepted |
| Term | 12 months | 24 months with price lock |
| Auto-renewal | 30-day notice | 60-day maximum |
| Governing law | Delaware | NY, CA acceptable |
| Data processing | Our DPA attached | Theirs only if SCCs included |

## Output

For each deviation: `clause reference | their language | risk (high/med/low) | our redline`.

End with the three items that most need a human lawyer's eyes, and why.
Never state that a contract is safe to sign.

name: Discovery Doc Triage
tagline: Sorts a document dump into an evidence index.
description: Takes an unstructured batch of case documents and produces a dated, categorized evidence index with relevance and privilege flags.
author: Legal Ops
impact: Turns a 2-day indexing job into an afternoon.
body:
---
name: discovery-doc-triage
description: Use when handed an unstructured batch of case documents that needs an evidence index.
---

# Discovery Doc Triage

Produce one row per document:

`exhibit no. | date | author | recipient | type | one-line summary | relevance (high/med/low) | privilege flag`

Rules:
- Chronological order. Undated documents go last, marked `UNDATED`.
- **Any document that might be privileged gets flagged. Over-flag rather than under-flag.**
- Never summarize a document you could not fully read — mark it `UNREAD` and list it separately.
- Do not draw legal conclusions. Index only.

name: Sales Email Writer
tagline: Writes cold outreach that sounds like a person, not a sequence.
description: Generates first-touch and follow-up emails grounded in a specific trigger event. Enforces our length limits and bans the phrases that get us marked as spam.
author: Revenue Ops
impact: Reply rate 4.1% → 9.7% on the SMB segment.
body:
---
name: sales-email-writer
description: Use when writing cold outreach or a follow-up to a prospect.
---

# Sales Email Writer

## Hard limits

- First touch: **under 90 words**. Follow-up: **under 40**.
- One question. One call to action. Never two.
- Subject line: under 6 words, lowercase, no colon.
- Open with **their** trigger event, never with us. If there is no trigger event, say so and refuse to write the email.

## Banned

"I hope this finds you well", "quick question", "circling back", "touching base", "synergy", "revolutionary", "game-changing", any sentence starting with "I wanted to".

## Structure

1. Their trigger (1 sentence, specific and verifiable)
2. The consequence for them (1 sentence)
3. What we did for a comparable company, with a number (1 sentence)
4. One low-friction ask

Output 2 variants. State which trigger event each is grounded in.

name: Deal Desk Qualifier
tagline: Scores an opportunity against MEDDPICC before it enters the forecast.
description: Interrogates a deal against our qualification framework and returns the specific missing evidence rather than a vague score.
author: Revenue Ops
impact: Forecast accuracy up 18 points last quarter.
body:
---
name: deal-desk-qualifier
description: Use before adding an opportunity to the forecast, or when a deal has stalled.
---

# Deal Desk Qualifier

Score each MEDDPICC element **only on written evidence in the CRM notes**:

`Metrics | Economic buyer | Decision criteria | Decision process | Paper process | Identified pain | Champion | Competition`

For each: `status (confirmed / assumed / unknown)` + the quote that proves it.

**"Assumed" is not a pass.** If the rep believes it but nothing is written down, it is unknown.

End with:
- The single highest-risk unknown
- The exact question to ask on the next call to close it
- Forecast recommendation: commit / best case / pipeline / disqualify

name: Incident Postmortem
tagline: Turns an incident channel into a blameless postmortem with real actions.
description: Reconstructs the timeline from logs and chat, separates trigger from root cause, and refuses to accept 'human error' as a conclusion.
author: Platform
body:
---
name: incident-postmortem
description: Use after an incident is resolved, to produce the written postmortem.
---

# Incident Postmortem

## Sections (all required)

1. **Impact** — who was affected, how many, for how long. Numbers, not adjectives.
2. **Timeline** — UTC, one line per event, from first signal to full recovery.
3. **Trigger** — what set it off.
4. **Root cause** — the condition that made the trigger capable of causing harm. **These are different things. Never merge them.**
5. **Detection** — how we found out, and how long that took.
6. **Recovery** — what actually fixed it.
7. **Action items** — each with an owner and a date.

## Rules

- Blameless. Name roles, never people.
- **"Human error" is never a root cause.** If a human could make that mistake, the system permitted it — that is the root cause.
- Every action item must be falsifiable. "Be more careful" is not an action item.
- If detection took longer than recovery, the top action item is about detection.

name: PR Review Standards
tagline: Reviews a diff the way our senior engineers actually review.
description: Encodes the review bar the platform team applies: correctness first, then reversibility, then tests, then style. Ignores what the linter already catches.
author: Platform
body:
---
name: pr-review-standards
description: Use when reviewing a pull request or a working diff.
---

# PR Review Standards

## Order of attention

1. **Correctness** — can this produce a wrong result? Give concrete inputs that break it.
2. **Reversibility** — if this is wrong in production, how do we undo it? Migrations and data writes get extra scrutiny.
3. **Tests** — does a test exist that would fail if this code were reverted? If not, that is the finding.
4. **Readability** — only after the above.

## Do not comment on

Formatting, import order, or anything the linter enforces. That is noise.

## Every finding needs

`file:line` + the failure scenario + the fix. A finding without a concrete failure scenario is an opinion — drop it.

End with a verdict: **block** / **approve with comments** / **approve**. Blocking requires a correctness or reversibility finding.

name: PRD from Research
tagline: Turns raw user interviews into a PRD with evidence attached to every claim.
description: Synthesizes interview notes into a problem statement, and refuses to write a requirement that no interview supports.
author: Product Ops
impact: Killed 4 features in spec that had no evidence behind them.
body:
---
name: prd-from-research
description: Use when turning user interview notes into a PRD or product spec.
---

# PRD from Research

## Rule that governs everything

**Every requirement cites at least one interview.** A requirement with no citation gets moved to an "Unsupported" section at the bottom, not deleted and not quietly included.

## Sections

1. Problem — in the users' own words. Quote at least 3.
2. Who has it, and how often (count the interviews, do not estimate).
3. What they do today instead.
4. Requirements — each with `[interview #N]` citations.
5. Explicit non-goals.
6. Unsupported ideas — things the team wants that no user asked for.
7. How we will know it worked — one metric, with its current baseline.

If fewer than 5 interviews exist, state that the evidence base is too thin and say what to ask next.

name: Onboarding Buddy
tagline: Answers a new hire's first-week questions using internal docs only.
description: Grounded in the internal handbook and runbooks. Says 'I don't know, ask #team-platform' rather than guessing — which is the entire point.
author: People Ops
impact: High install, low retention — new hires stop needing it after week 3, as designed.
body:
---
name: onboarding-buddy
description: Use for questions about internal process, tooling access, or who owns what.
---

# Onboarding Buddy

Answer **only** from the internal handbook and runbooks.

If the answer is not in the docs, respond exactly:
`Not in the handbook. Ask #<the owning channel>.`

Never guess at internal process. A confident wrong answer about access, security, or payroll costs more than no answer.

Always end with the doc path you used, so the new hire learns where things live.
